title: A week in Duke Ellington's lax band and quitting over unpaid salary
summary: After Cab's discipline, Duke's undermanned, late-starting band and half pay made him quit after a week.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: But I was very much disappointed. After leaving Cab's band, you know, which was a well disciplined band, I went to Duke's band, which was very lax.
Well, you stayed with Cab from 1946 to what?
So anyway, I joined Duke, and from staying with Cab Calloway and the way his band was run, the first night, we opened up at the Shea Buffalo Auditorium --

or, no, it was the City Auditorium in Buffalo, New York, and we opened up with something like 7 pieces, and there was Duke sitting up there with a big smile on his face just like nothing happened, and I'm about to blow my top, because in Calloway's band, this did not happen.

So I didn't say anything about it, but the next night we played in Hamilton, Ontario, and the same thing happened. So I said to Clark Terry, who was in the band at the time, I said to Clark Terry, "Does this happen all the time?" and he said, "Well, yeah, you know -- Duke doesn't If a cat comes up late, he doesn't say nothin'." say anything." I said, "Well, man, this would never happen in Cab's band, I tell you that -- everybody would be fired before you could shake your head. I don't think I'm gonna like it here."
So, after a week in the band, the road manager -- can I call his name?

Yeah, Sully. The road manager, Sully, came up and paid me half of my salary, which was another thing that didn't happen in Cab's band, because in Cab Calloway's band, he had two envelopes -- a white one and a blue one, and the blue one, in fact, before I tell you about the blue one, he used to always tell you, "Don't grumble on stay; and and stage, grumble or be on your way or wait until Thursday -- that was payday in Cab's band.

Now if you got a blue envelope, you knew you had two more weeks to go, but if you got that white envelope, there was a ticket in there, 9 out of 10 times, there was a ticket in there and your notice to leave.

So when Sully came up with half of my salary, because at that time, Duke was going through some sort of transition there with the band, and he was having problems as far as the finances went, and so he paid me half of my money, and I said, 'Well, where's the rest of it?' and he said, 'Well, we'll give it to you in a couple of days' and I said, 'No man, I want all my money. I was here and I made my time, I did my work, and I expect to be paid'.

So he said, 'Well, we'll give it to you in a couple of days' and, I said, 'Well, I tell you what you do -- when we get to Chicago (this was in Toledo, Ohio) you get you another drummer, I'm going home'.

So I left the band -- I was only in the band for a week, I didn't stay no longer than a week, but I guess because of me working with Cab, I was just, you know, I was so used to things being run right, to my way of thinking, that I just couldn't stand to be in a band where I open up with an arrangement for 15 pieces and we got six on the bandstand.
